A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SageAttention3 and SageBwd work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised and added content.

before.justification: v1 reports original attention-kernel benchmarks, image/video generation evaluations, language-model fine-tuning and pretraining results, and five-seed experiments in Appendix A.4.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds combined training/inference experiments, INT8-versus-FP8 comparisons, and layerwise-error and smoothing analyses.

M1.justification: The core quantization designs remain. Algorithms 1–2 correct the running-normalizer and output-rescaling recurrences, and Algorithm 3 adds smooth-K gradient compensation. K smoothing itself was already described in v1. Appendix A.6 additionally tests an inference variant keeping three sensitive layers in FP16; these are limited procedural revisions, not a redesign.

E1.justification: The evaluated data and tasks remain Open-Sora prompts, COCO, GSM8K, DROP, MMLU, HellaSwag and FineWeb-Edu across the retained language, image and video models. The added precision combinations change configurations within this coverage. B200/B300 throughput estimates do not establish new empirical hardware scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluated alternatives: FP8 SageBwd becomes a gradient and fine-tuning comparator in Tables 6–8; SmoothQuant and Hadamard transformations enter the smoothing comparison in Table 16; and FlashAttention3 variants enter the accuracy comparison in Table 18. The original benchmark comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 add 1,000-step Qwen fine-tuning followed by FP4 inference and explicitly hold dOV^T in FP16 for the INT8/FP8 comparisons. These are additional evaluation protocols. Appendix A.3 retains the original 700-step fine-tuning settings, metrics and pretraining configuration, so the PDFs do not establish changes to those experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained format, scaling and backward-precision ablations, v2 adds INT8/FP8 gradient analysis, accumulated-error analysis with selective FP16 mitigation, comparisons of smoothing strategies, and throughput/accuracy trade-off analyses (Section 5.4 and Appendices A.6–A.9). These substantially broaden investigation of precision choices and error mechanisms.

E5.justification: Figure 3's uncertainty displays and Appendix A.4's five seeds, averages and standard deviations are retained. The seed tables are merely renumbered from 5–10 to 9–14. The added checklist restates existing reporting; no additional uncertainty-estimation procedure or increased run count is disclosed.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–4, figures and seed-table values are retained, but substantial new results appear. Under the new FP4-inference setup, Table 5 reports Qwen2.5-1.5B GSM8K accuracy of 0.5232 after INT8 versus 0.4912 after BF16 fine-tuning. Table 6 reports dQ L1 error of 0.0290 for INT8 versus 0.0696 for FP8. Layerwise, smoothing and throughput/accuracy results are also added; these are not improvements over the original evaluation under identical settings.

T1.justification: v1 mentions a formal two-level-quantization analysis but supplies no corresponding appendix derivation. v2 adds relative-error definitions and a representable-level proof argument in A.10, plus Gaussian/independence assumptions and a first-order gradient-error derivation in A.11. The corrected softmax recurrences also revise the mathematical specification.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: FP4 inference attention reaching 1038 TOPS and approximately 5× FlashAttention speedup, and trainable low-bit attention preserving fine-tuning performance while converging more slowly in pretraining. The added evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds a hypothesis that INT8 fine-tuning reduces distribution mismatch with FP4 inference, interprets decreasing errors in some deeper layers as partial cancellation, and discusses selective FP16 mitigation. It also motivates INT8 through gradient accuracy and broader hardware support. These extend the interpretation while retaining the original pretraining limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 newly documents fusing V transposition into the quantization kernel to avoid additional memory traffic. The abstract changes code availability from promised to available, and the new experiments disclose their training duration and precision control. The transpose discussion does not establish that the original implementation changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including an efficient-attention survey, SageAttention2++, SLA, SparseVideoGen2, SmoothQuant, AWQ and hardware documentation, while removing UniFormer. The related-work framework and central novelty positioning remain largely unchanged; these are targeted contextual additions.

P1.justification: Most original prose and its organization are retained. v2 adds Sections 5.3–5.4, further appendix subsections, acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist, alongside small wording and cross-reference edits. Author order, affiliations and conference information also change. This extends the document without extensive rewriting of its existing narrative.

P2.justification: Tables 5–8 and 15–18 add substantial displays for combined training/inference, gradient comparisons, layerwise errors, smoothing and throughput/accuracy trade-offs. Existing Figures 1–21 are retained, and the original seed tables are renumbered and reflowed. The major visual change is the expanded tabular evidence, rather than redrawn figures or pagination alone.

improvement.justification: Corrected algorithm recurrences, controlled INT8/FP8 comparisons, new error and smoothing analyses, and implementation disclosure improve technical clarity and empirical support. The gains are limited by weaknesses in the added theory: A.10's representable-value counts do not establish its strict error inequality, and A.11's expectation argument does not by itself establish error-magnitude dominance. Overall, the empirical and documentation gains support a modest improvement.
